map.sentence: Google Cloud announced the Gemini agent on Oct 8 at its Gemini at Work 2026 event, calling it "a universal agent for work".
Google says the agent plans a job, uses tools, connects to a company's systems and brings back finished work inside the documents, inbox and developer tools people already use.
Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian made the pitch in his keynote: "You give it objectives, not instructions. You delegate an outcome and come back to finished work".
map.support: Full two-sentence quote in the Cloud post authored by Kurian and adapted from his keynote (factcheck).

map.sentence: (same sentence as above, second citation: keynote attribution)
map.support: factcheck: Computerworld quotes the first sentence as said 'in his keynote'.

map.sentence: It claims nearly 80% of Google Cloud customers use its AI products and nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 use Gemini Enterprise.
We found no independent test of the agent in the coverage reviewed.
map.note: Revision 3 cut the duplicate TechCrunch early-testers clause; C17 stays cited in 'Who gets it, and when'.
map.support: First clause: dossier-news.md 'Nothing has been independently tested or benchmarked', reworded per factcheck as a limit on the coverage reviewed.

map.sentence: Google says Gemini can create "a roster of sub-agents," short-lived helpers that each have their own identity, for multi-step work that "can run for hours or days".
It keeps four kinds of memory: session, semantic, procedural and episodic.
It can reach business tools and databases, plus any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a shared format for connecting AI agents to other software.
map.support: The MCP definition is the writer's gloss. The fact-checker confirmed it against modelcontextprotocol.io.

map.sentence: Google says it routes jobs across its Gemini models and "Claude models from Anthropic today," with other models to come.
TechCrunch reports a "tasks inbox" where users can watch the agent's thinking, its hand-offs to sub-agents and its progress.
A "coworker agent" gets its own Workspace account, with an email address, calendar, Drive and a listing in the company directory, Google says.
Every action is "written to an audit trail and attributed to the agent rather than to a person".
Each agent also gets a cryptographically attested identity, a digital ID that can be verified, and only the permissions its job needs.
Agents run in a sandbox, and their traffic passes through Agent Gateway, which Google calls an AI network firewall that enforces company policy in real time.
If a project hits its spending cap, its agent pauses.

Mahmoud Ramin of Info-Tech Research Group noted, per Computerworld, that the launch does not create a whole new category, since OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Meta already offer multi-agent features.
map.support: Paraphrase, not a direct quote, per factcheck.

map.sentence: He added that an autonomous agent with reach into many business systems carries more risk, so guardrails must be enforced.
Independent analyst Carmi Levy said Google is trying to establish itself as the gatekeeper of the new enterprise operating system.
map.support: Follows the article's wording, per factcheck. No quote marks.

map.sentence: Whether company tech and security chiefs "can trust it to run mission critical business processes indefinitely without doing something stupid enough to generate damaging headlines is another story altogether," he said.
map.support: 'company tech and security chiefs' paraphrases 'CIOs and CISOs' outside the quote marks.

map.sentence: TechCrunch reports that On, Shopify and PayPal were early testers, and that Google will bring the agent to businesses before consumers.
9to5Google says it is in private preview, with wide availability "soon" for select Workspace Business and Enterprise plans.
Constellation Research reports general availability is expected around the end of October or early November, with consumption pricing to follow later.
Google's own posts give no date or price.
map.support: dossier-news.md 'Unverified / gaps'. The fact-checker verified it (pass).

map.sentence: Versions tuned for financial services and legal work are in preview, Google says.
A Hacker News post linking Google's announcement had 18 points and 2 comments as of Oct 10.
AI agents can judge a proposed action well but do far worse when they must investigate and carry it out themselves, a new preprint finds.
Hongzhan Lin, Shidong Cao and four co-authors posted the paper, which is not yet peer-reviewed, on Oct 6.
map.support: Shidong Cao is named in dossier-research.md §3.

map.sentence: Their core point: "correct outcomes do not guarantee that their actions were supported by evidence established beforehand".
An agent that reaches the right outcome without first establishing the evidence still fails their test.
map.support: Restates the abstract's point using the factcheck's wording. No citation: it explains the sentence before it.

map.sentence: The team built SafeActBench, 656 synthetic cases in six areas of work, including customer and policy operations, legal and financial work, smart-home control and healthcare operations.
They tested five models: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash and GLM-5.2.
Each ran in its maker's own agent app, such as Claude Code or Codex, and in a shared test setup, for ten configurations in all.
A deterministic evaluator, a fixed rule-checker rather than another AI acting as judge, scored every run.
"Reading $49.99 from charge C1 does not establish the amount of C2, even when the values match," the project page explains.
95% vs. 52%. In three setups re-tested on the same 100 cases, judging accuracy was 95% to 99% but success at doing the work was 28% to 52%.
map.support: factcheck: Sec 5.2 and Table 9 report DeepSeek-Inspect 95.0 vs 52.0, GLM-Inspect 97.0 vs 28.0 and GLM-ZCode 99.0 vs 33.0, each on 100 cases.

map.sentence: 12.1%. GLM-5.2 in its own ZCode app scored above 96% on the judging test, then fell to between 12.1% and 34.1% on the action tests.
21.7% to 62.9%. In cases where the right move was to investigate and then decline, this is how often agents stopped investigating too early.
37.0% to 66.9%. Among single-action runs where an agent acted, this is the share where it acted before the required evidence was in place.
93.2% to 100%. Once the evidence was complete, nine of ten configurations carried out the action correctly at these rates.
About half. When the researchers withheld one decisive record, agents still acted in 46.5% to 53.5% of those runs.
So agents stumble in the investigation before an action, while the action itself mostly goes right.
When the requester said a missing record had already been checked and was fine, agents acted less often, not more.
map.support: dossier-research.md §5 'Requester-claim condition' (6/43, 10/43, 6/43). Context for r16.

map.sentence: The authors write that agents "respond more to a requester's conflicting claim than to absent evidence alone".
DeepSeek gained 4.4 points in its own app, while GLM did 6.8 points worse in ZCode.
The test worlds are synthetic, and the authors say results "should not be interpreted as certifications of safety for deployed systems".
The people who checked the evaluator were "members of the research team".
Their audit of 300 runs found it wrongly accepted 2.0% of its positive judgments (3 of 150) and wrongly rejected 1.3% of its negative ones (2 of 150).
map.support: factcheck: App B.3 gives these per-class counts.

map.sentence: The method sees what an agent visibly did, not what it relied on internally.
In a class-balanced control, the judging-versus-doing gap shrank to about 5 to 13 points in most setups (22 in one), and one setup did better at doing than judging.
map.support: factcheck: App C.2.1 Table 10 shows Claude-Inspect at 22.2 and GLM-Inspect at 83.8 interactive vs 73.7 static.

map.sentence: A method the authors tried for structuring evidence, SCGR-Select, which they describe as a training-free analysis instrument, did not reliably help: "structured evidence selection alone does not ensure higher task success".
map.support: factcheck: the paper calls SCGR a 'lightweight, training-free analysis instrument'.

map.sentence: IBM Research's Near-Miss study found hidden policy failures in 8% to 17% of runs where agents used tools that change data, "even when the final outcome matches the expected ground-truth state".
The authors name extending their evidence-withholding tests to multi-action tasks as a natural next step.
map.support: Conclusion: 'Extending the interventions to multi-action protocols ... is a natural next step.'

map.sentence: Their code (MIT license) and data (CC BY 4.0) are public, so others can check the results.
Big Arrow on the Screen lets an AI agent draw a big arrow, box or text sign on top of every window.
The open-source Mac tool comes from developer Franz Enzenhofer.
map.support: LICENSE: 'Copyright (c) 2026 Franz Enzenhofer' (verified by the fact-checker). Developer name also in dossier-invention.md 'Who'.

map.sentence: Its README sums it up: "It never clicks, types or captures. It only points. Deliberately."
Its Show HN post from Oct 9 had 368 points and 161 comments on Hacker News as of Oct 10.
map.support: Counts from the fact-checker's live check (368 points, 161 comments, item created 2026-10-09T11:03:48Z, submitter franze). The ledger records 366.

map.sentence: It is a command-line tool plus a skill, an add-on set of instructions, for Claude Code and Codex.
Clicks pass through the arrow, keyboard focus stays put, and the arrow removes itself.
It is meant for steps "only a human may do," or ones the person wants to learn.
The author noted on Hacker News that Claude refuses some actions, such as entering passwords or changing security settings, even when given broad permissions.
It is one Swift program with "no telemetry" and, the README says, "no AI inside".
Drawing needs no Mac permission.
The overlay is a window set to ignore the mouse and sit at the screen-saver level,
which an Apple developer-support answer says is needed to stay above full-screen apps.
Arrows disappear after 8 seconds for a quick point or 300 seconds for a longer one, or when the agent that drew them exits.
Pointing at a button by its label needs Accessibility permission for the terminal that launched the tool.
One commenter called it a "'Guiding agent' rather than 'doing agent'".
It runs only on macOS 14 or later.
It is days old, and the author's figures, including 104 automated tests and 1.4% CPU use, are self-reported.
map.support: 'days old' and 'self-reported' come from dossier-invention.md status and caveats (first commit 2026-10-08).

map.sentence: It contains no AI of its own, so an agent has to call it from the command line.
One critic on Hacker News put the deeper problem plainly: "An arrow on the screen solves 'where do I click'; it doesn't solve 'should this happen'".
The tool's skill tells the agent to write on the sign what a click will do when it approves, pays or deletes something.
The README's listed tests cover geometry, placement and timing, not what the sign says, so that rests on the agent following the instruction.
map.support: The inv-09 test list covers geometry, placement, joints, golden image, copy buttons, click-through, focus and stop timing. Sign content is not on it.

map.sentence: Another commenter said it "seems great for scammers targeting old people".
The author's answer is that an agent running shell commands "can do far worse" already.
Google is selling agents that run multi-step business jobs for hours or days.
The SafeActBench team found that agents' weak spot is the checking before an action, though their paper did not test Google's agent.
Big Arrow takes the cautious route: the agent points, and a person clicks.
